about: Build the shared chart dataset for the data visualization round (November 6, 2026; DR-44 to DR-51).
source_line_order: publisher, title or table, observation period, geography, date retrieved, qualification

specimens.reader_question: Do Republicans and Democrats agree on anything about Congress?
specimens.requirements: One figure set large, the two party figures beside it with names printed, and the House and Senate votes as context. Party marks in neutral inks (DR-48).

specimens.reader_question: What happened to child poverty when the expanded child tax credit was paid, and after it lapsed?
specimens.requirements: One series in Charcoal, events as notes inside the plot, the unit once, a true minus where needed, the Census revision stated. The title must not credit one policy alone.

specimens.reader_question: Who changed the rules: voters, courts or legislatures?
specimens.requirements: Bars start at zero, direct labels, the grouping note printed. Optional: split each bar by direction without red.

specimens.reader_question: Which age groups vote, and did that change between two elections?
specimens.requirements: Two years per row, the change labeled in words and numbers, survey self-report qualified.

specimens.reader_question: How far apart are homeownership rates by race, and has the gap closed?
specimens.requirements: One panel per group, one shared scale (or the subtitle says otherwise), each panel highlights its group over the others in Stone.

specimens.reader_question: If a reform path were followed, which way would each outcome move?
specimens.requirements: V7's words print in every cell; any glyph or tint follows the class method and is labeled as the studio's reading. Tests the diverging pair without red and blue.

specimens.reader_question: Where can a city adopt ranked-choice voting, and where has the state ruled it out?
specimens.requirements: Categorical, with words in the key and on hover, a table equivalent listing every state, and the as-of date in the title or measure line.

specimens.reader_question: Have the rules been moving toward voters or away from them?
specimens.requirements: One mark per repair-log row, keyed by its RL id; direction by shape or position as well as tint; the coding note one click or one line away.

specimens.reader_question: Which rule changes since 1870 decided who counts, who governs, who owns and who checks?
specimens.requirements: Four thread lanes, dates on a true time scale, event names printed, every event documented.

specimens.reader_question: How much of each everyday answer rests on documented fact?
specimens.requirements: A share per question across four grades, sorted, with grades readable in grayscale and never in red.

rows.rule: The Voting Rights Act banned discriminatory voting tests and required places with a history of discrimination to get federal approval (preclearance) before changing voting rules.
rows.margin: statute (House 333-85, Senate 77-19 on initial passage; P.L. 89-110)
rows.reversed_by: Shelby County v. Holder, June 25, 2013, disabled preclearance; Louisiana v. Callais, April 29, 2026, narrowed Section 2
rows.source_title: Voting Rights Act (1965) - National Archives; vote counts from Wikipedia

rows.rule: New York City Local Law 8 of 1988 created the Campaign Finance Board and a public matching-funds program for small contributions, first paid at 1 to 1 in 1989 and raised to 4 to 1 in 1998, 6 to 1 in 2007 and 8 to 1 from 2019. A charter referendum on November 8, 1988 then made the Board an independent agency under the City Charter, so a later Council could not simply repeal it.
rows.margin: local law (Local Law 8 of 1988, signed February 29, 1988); the November 8, 1988 charter questions all passed, and the vote count for each question is not in the digitized record
rows.source_title: CFB Milestones, New York City Campaign Finance Board

rows.rule: Citizens United v. FEC held that limits on independent political spending by corporations and unions violate the First Amendment.
rows.source_title: Citizens United v. FEC, 558 U.S. 310 (2010) - Justia

rows.rule: Shelby County v. Holder struck down the Section 4(b) coverage formula, ending Section 5 preclearance in practice.

rows.rule: McCutcheon v. FEC struck down aggregate limits on how much one donor may give to all federal candidates and parties combined.
rows.source_title: McCutcheon v. FEC, 572 U.S. 185 (2014) - Justia

rows.rule: HB 2177 made Oregon the first state to register eligible voters automatically from driver license records. By the National Conference of State Legislatures' count of August 19, 2026, 24 states and the District of Columbia have enacted or put in place automatic voter registration.

rows.rule: Question 5 adopted ranked-choice voting, in which voters rank candidates and ballots transfer when a first choice is eliminated, for state and federal primaries and for general elections for U.S. Senate, U.S. House, governor and the legislature.
rows.reversed_by: The legislature passed LD 1646 on October 23, 2017, delaying ranked-choice voting and repealing it automatically by December 1, 2021 unless the constitution was amended; voters overturned LD 1646 by people's veto on June 12, 2018

rows.rule: LD 1646 delayed ranked-choice voting until December 2021 and repealed it automatically unless voters amended the state constitution.
rows.reversed_by: People's veto, Question 1, approved June 12, 2018 (53.88%), overturning LD 1646

rows.rule: Proposal 2 created a 13-member independent citizens redistricting commission to draw congressional and legislative maps.

rows.rule: Proposition 4 created an independent redistricting commission and banned partisan gerrymandering in the drawing of congressional and legislative districts.

rows.rule: Utah S.B. 200 turned the redistricting commission created by Proposition 4 into a seven-member advisory body appointed largely by legislative leaders, and let the Legislature vote on or adopt a commission map without being required to. rule-changes.intro: The repair log records 64 dated changes to the rules that decide who officials answer to: statutes, court rulings, ballot measures, executive actions and local laws from 1965 to the November 3, 2026 ballot. Each row gives the jurisdiction, what the rule did, the vote or margin, the instrument used, the feedback loop it acts on and anything that later reversed or limited it. Changes run in both directions and come from both parties. One row rests on a source that was not checked, and the row is labelled.
rule-changes.coding_note: Each row is coded by one of five labels. 'Toward voters' means the change widens who can register, vote or have a ballot counted, makes each vote weigh more equally, opens the contest that decides the seat, makes political money more limited or more visible, strengthens an independent check on officials, or adds to household security through automatic benefits. 'Away from voters' means the change does the reverse. 'Voters kept existing rules' means a ballot measure failed and the rules in force stayed, coded the same whichever way the measure would have moved power. 'Pending' means voters or courts have not yet decided. 'Mixed' means the change moved in both directions at once or left the rules in practice unchanged; the row's own note says which. Three rules apply across parties. A partisan redraw of district maps in the middle of a decade is coded away from voters whichever party draws it and whether or not voters approved it; a court order that blocks one is coded toward voters, and one that lets it take effect is coded away. A change that widens who takes part in the deciding round (open or all-party primaries) or lets voters rank candidates is coded toward voters, and a law or amendment that bans those options is coded away; readers may weigh these entries differently, and the reform profiles R-01 and R-02 rate confidence in their effect on moderation as low. A row's direction describes the rule's effect on who officials answer to and carries no judgment of the people or parties involved.
rule-changes.source_line: Oath & Action, Who Do They Answer To? Systems Atlas V7, repair log of 64 dated rule changes. August 6, 1965 to the November 3, 2026 ballot. scenarios-2030.title: Eight scenarios and the direction each would move four outcome families
scenarios-2030.class_method: The studio's coarse reading of V7's direction words, for a glyph or tint only. The words are V7's and always print beside any glyph. Words that start 'up' read up; 'slightly up' and 'small and slow' read slightly up; 'flat', 'near trend' and 'flat through 2036' read flat; 'down or flat' and 'flat, or down if ...' read flat or down; 'down' reads down; 'mixed' and 'prices down ...; employment effects mixed' read mixed; 'same as scenario ii' points to scenario ii.

rows.name: Baseline: no reform beyond current law
assumptions: Current law, including the 2025 budget law (P.L. 119-21) and P.L. 119-75, runs as written
The Senate keeps the legislative filibuster
Recent trends in executive action and court rulings continue
watch: Top 1% share of wealth each quarter
rows.DQ_why: Mid-decade redraws and the narrower Section 2 standard after Louisiana v. Callais raise C4: Officeholders' control over election rules. The Federal Election Commission stays without a quorum.
rows.GE_why: Workforce losses, funding lapses and closed digital service teams weigh on D5: Quality of public services.
rows.EP_why: Productivity grows near its recent trend; tariffs add costs.
rows.EQ_why: Stock prices push the top 1% share to records, and the 2025 law shifts resources toward higher-income households.

rows.name: State and local track by 2030
assumptions: Initiatives and statutes pass in some states: nomination rules, local elections moved onto the statewide calendar, housing allowed by right, wage floors and child credits
Federal administrative capacity is restored only if the administration that takes office in 2029 chooses to restore it
watch: Housing permits per 1,000 residents in reform metros
rows.DQ_why: C2: How often the primary decides the winner falls where nomination rules change, and local turnout rises when local elections share the ballot with statewide contests.
rows.GE_why: State capacity rises where it is funded; federal capacity follows the administration.
rows.EP: slightly up in metro areas that reform housing rules
rows.EP_why: New housing supply takes three to ten years to arrive.
rows.EQ: up for renters and low-income families in reform states
rows.EQ_why: Wage floors, credits and housing supply help; top shares barely move.

rows.name: A coherent federal package
assumptions: A Senate majority changes the filibuster and uses the change first on rules for elections and government
Statutes pass on the civil service, inspectors general, emergency powers, tariffs and public research
A permanent refundable child credit passes through budget reconciliation
watch: Child poverty under the Supplemental Poverty Measure
Share of IRS phone calls answered
Appropriations bills passed through regular order
rows.DQ: up on structure; uncertain on behavior
rows.DQ_why: Maps, the visibility of political money and the schedule of court appointments change; evidence that any of it lowers affective polarization is weak.
rows.GE_why: Capacity measures have the best-identified evidence and work through administration in two to five years.
rows.EP_why: Public research pays off over decades; competition measures act one sector at a time.
rows.EQ: up quickly on income; slowly on wealth
rows.EQ_why: Transfers act in the year they pay, as in 2021; taxes on capital act over decades.

rows.name: Parties first: fusion voting and public funding for parties
assumptions: R-47: Allow fusion voting and consider public support for parties, and R-07: Match small donations or give voters campaign vouchers, adopted widely
rows.DQ_why: Coalitions can form without one candidate splitting the vote of another (the spoiler problem).
rows.GE: same as scenario ii (state and local track)
rows.EP: same as scenario ii (state and local track)
rows.EQ: same as scenario ii (state and local track)

rows.name: Capacity first: civil service, IRS, inspectors general, congressional staff and digital service
assumptions: R-17: Protect a professional career civil service; R-27: Rebuild skilled enforcement of taxes already owed; R-15: Give watchdogs usable remedies when oversight is obstructed; R-13: Rebuild Congress's own expertise; R-39: Build public teams that can deliver digital services
rows.GE_why: A change made by statute lasts; one made by executive order can be undone by the next order.
rows.EP: same as scenario ii (state and local track)
rows.EQ_why: More revenue is collected, and existing benefits reach more of the people eligible for them.

rows.name: Competition and labor first
assumptions: R-19: Address drug-middleman conflicts and sector-specific market power; R-20: Enforce merger rules in markets for goods and labor; R-21: Make labor-law remedies timely and help secure first contracts; R-22: Set industry-wide standards through bargaining or wage boards; R-38: Limit competitors' use of shared private data to set prices; R-44: Open digital platform markets to effective competition
rows.DQ: slightly up if union membership rises
rows.DQ_why: Through Loop R15: Unions, civic ties and equal turnout reinforce each other, run in reverse: stronger unions sustain organizations that bring people into civic life.
rows.EP: prices down in affected sectors; employment effects mixed

rows.name: Constitutional amendments
assumptions: R-50: Assess constitutional representation changes and the popular-vote compact, and R-16: Regular Supreme Court appointments and enforceable ethics, adopted by constitutional amendment under Article V
rows.DQ_why: Supermajorities of the size Article V requires are unlikely to form by 2036.

rows.name: Forbearance: restraint by officials without new rules
assumptions: Officials restrain themselves without new rules
rows.DQ: flat, or down if one side stops holding back
rows.DQ_why: Unwritten norms bind only while both sides keep them.

scenarios-2030.intro: Each scenario states a set of assumptions and gives the direction each outcome family would take if those assumptions hold. These are conditional directions. They make no forecast of what will happen and give no odds that any assumption comes true. The four outcome families are read separately and never added together. A scenario shows a number only when it names the method and the inputs behind it.
scenarios-2030.source_line: Oath & Action, Who Do They Answer To? Systems Atlas V7, reform outcomes, eight scenarios. Conditional directions to 2036 from a 2026 baseline. United States. Snapshot of 2026-10-15. Each scenario gives a direction only if its assumptions hold. It is no forecast, gives no odds, and the four families are never added together.
notes: Title verbs take "would" or "may": these are conditional estimates (section 15).

history-events.title: Twenty-four changes in the rules, 1870 to 2026, on four threads

threads.label: Who counts
threads.question: Who gets to vote, and whose vote counts fully?

threads.label: Who governs
threads.question: How do votes become seats, nominees and majorities?

threads.label: Who owns
threads.question: How do rules decide who keeps the gains and who carries the risk?

threads.label: Who checks
threads.question: Who can see an abuse of power, and who can stop it?

rows.title: Fifteenth Amendment ratified
rows.mechanism: Barred race as a voting qualification and left enforcement to Congress and the courts.
rows.loop: Loop R4b: Voting rules shape who can hold rule-makers accountable

rows.title: Mississippi adopts its 1890 constitution
rows.mechanism: Literacy tests, poll taxes and understanding clauses (which let registrars judge whether an applicant could explain the constitution) spread across the South, and Black registration collapsed within a decade.
rows.loop: Loop R4b: Voting rules shape who can hold rule-makers accountable
rows.source_text: Mississippi Constitution of 1890, art. 12; Kousser, The Shaping of Southern Politics (1974)

rows.title: Seventeenth Amendment ratified
rows.mechanism: Senators became directly elected; each state kept two senators regardless of population.
rows.loop: Loop R12: Entrenched majorities shape courts that rule on election rules

rows.title: Nineteenth Amendment ratified
rows.mechanism: Barred sex as a voting qualification; the eligible electorate roughly doubled on paper.
rows.loop: Loop B4: Electoral consequences can improve public performance

rows.title: Reapportionment Act of 1929 fixes the House at 435
rows.mechanism: Average district size grew from about 210,000 to about 760,000 people, which reduced constituents' access to their member and how closely seats track population.
rows.loop: Outside driver X2: Population patterns and residential sorting (no named loop); related reform R-46: Expand the House of Representatives

rows.title: Wagner Act (and the Social Security Act, August 14, 1935)
rows.mechanism: Created collective bargaining rights and social insurance, with agricultural and domestic workers excluded.
rows.loop: Loop R6: Weak bargaining power and concentrated wealth reinforce each other

rows.title: Taft-Hartley Act passed over a veto
rows.mechanism: Allowed state right-to-work laws and barred secondary boycotts; union growth stopped in the South.
rows.loop: Loop R6: Weak bargaining power and concentrated wealth reinforce each other

rows.title: Reynolds v. Sims (with Baker v. Carr, 1962, and Wesberry v. Sanders, 1964)
rows.mechanism: Established one person, one vote for state legislatures and House districts, ending the overrepresentation of rural areas.
rows.loop: Loop B4: Electoral consequences can improve public performance

rows.title: Voting Rights Act signed
rows.mechanism: Required federal approval (preclearance) of voting changes in covered places and sent federal examiners; Black registration in the South rose from about 30% to over 60% by 1970.
rows.loop: Loop R4b: Voting rules shape who can hold rule-makers accountable

rows.title: McGovern-Fraser rules take effect
rows.mechanism: Binding primaries and caucuses replaced bargaining at party conventions, so primary voters became the people who choose nominees.
rows.loop: Loop R10: Safe seats shift accountability to small primary electorates
rows.source_text: Commission on Party Structure and Delegate Selection, Mandate for Reform (1970); Shafer, Quiet Revolution (1983)

rows.title: Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act (Federal Election Campaign Act amendments, October 15, 1974)
rows.mechanism: Made it unlawful for the President to withhold appropriated money without a rescission approved by Congress; the campaign-finance amendments set contribution limits and created the Federal Election Commission.
rows.loop: Loop R18: Weakening watchdogs lowers the cost of further unilateral action

rows.title: Buckley v. Valeo
rows.mechanism: Struck down spending limits and kept contribution limits; treating campaign money as speech has framed the law for fifty years.
rows.loop: Loop R1b: Political spending and court rulings reinforce each other

rows.title: Proposition 13 (labor-law reform filibustered June 22, 1978; First National Bank of Boston v. Bellotti, April 26, 1978)
rows.mechanism: The California tax revolt, the defeat of labor-law reform in the Senate and new corporate speech rights arrived in one season.
rows.loop: Loop R1: Wealth and political influence reinforce each other
rows.source_text: Cal. Const. art. XIII A; 124 Cong. Rec. 18,398 (1978); 435 U.S. 765

rows.title: Inspector General Act (Ethics in Government Act, October 26, 1978)
rows.mechanism: Created statutory watchdogs inside agencies and required financial disclosure by officials.
rows.loop: Loop B1a: Independent oversight can limit policy favoritism

rows.title: The 104th Congress opens
rows.mechanism: The House cut committee staff by about 41% (2,147 in 1993 to 1,266 in 1995), Congress closed the Office of Technology Assessment and party leaders took more control; expectations that committee members raise money followed.
rows.loop: Loop R2: Congress becomes dependent on outside expertise
rows.source_text: H.Res. 6 (104th); Brookings Vital Statistics on Congress, ch. 5

rows.title: Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (Commodity Futures Modernization Act, December 21, 2000)
rows.mechanism: Allowed banks, securities firms and insurers to combine, and the 2000 law left most derivatives unregulated; the 2008 crisis and the TARP bank rescue followed.
rows.loop: Loop R1: Wealth and political influence reinforce each other

rows.title: Citizens United v. FEC (SpeechNow.org v. FEC, March 26, 2010)
rows.mechanism: Independent spending by corporations and unions became unlimited; super PACs followed within two months.
rows.loop: Loop R1b: Political spending and court rulings reinforce each other

rows.title: Shelby County v. Holder
rows.mechanism: Struck down the formula that decided which places needed preclearance, which ended preclearance in practice; Texas moved to enforce its voter-ID law the same day.
rows.loop: Loop R4b: Voting rules shape who can hold rule-makers accountable

rows.title: Nuclear option for lower-court and executive nominations (extended to the Supreme Court on April 6, 2017)
rows.mechanism: A rules change by simple majority ended the 60-vote threshold for these confirmations, so appointments track which party controls the Senate.
rows.loop: Loop R12: Entrenched majorities shape courts that rule on election rules
rows.source_text: Congressional Record, Nov. 21, 2013, S8417; Apr. 6, 2017, S2390

rows.title: Tax Cuts and Jobs Act
rows.mechanism: Cut the corporate rate to 21% and made the individual cuts temporary; the resulting deficits fed later arguments for spending cuts.
rows.loop: Loop R1: Wealth and political influence reinforce each other

rows.title: Electoral Count Reform Act
rows.mechanism: Made the Vice President's role in the count ministerial, required one-fifth of each chamber to raise an objection, made governors' certificates conclusive and sped up court review.
rows.loop: Loop B4: Electoral consequences can improve public performance

rows.title: 2025 budget reconciliation law, P.L. 119-21 (counter-event: the American Rescue Plan, March 11, 2021)
rows.mechanism: The 2025 law extends the 2017 tax cuts and, by Congressional Budget Office estimates tallied by KFF, cuts federal Medicaid spending by about $1 trillion over 2025 to 2034, with further cuts to SNAP food aid. The 2021 law expanded the child tax credit for one year, when child poverty under the Supplemental Poverty Measure fell to 5.2%; the expansion then expired.
rows.loop: Loop R5: Financial strain narrows who takes part in policy decisions

rows.title: Louisiana v. Callais
rows.mechanism: The Supreme Court (6 to 3) held that Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is violated only when the evidence supports a strong inference of intentional discrimination. Within five weeks Florida, Tennessee and Louisiana enacted new congressional maps and the Court let Alabama return to its 2023 plan; each change removed a majority-Black or Black-opportunity district.
rows.loop: Loop R4b: Voting rules shape who can hold rule-makers accountable

rows.title: Trump v. Slaughter and Trump v. Cook (NRSC v. FEC, June 30, 2026; inspector general removals, January 24, 2025; Storch v. Hegseth ruling, September 24, 2025)
rows.mechanism: Trump v. Slaughter overruled Humphrey's Executor and lets the President remove Federal Trade Commission members at will (6 to 3). The same day, in Trump v. Cook, the Court (5 to 4) declined to let the President remove Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook while her case continues, an interim order. On June 30, 2026, NRSC v. FEC struck down limits on party committees' coordinated spending. At least 17 inspectors general were removed on January 24, 2025 without the required notice; on September 24, 2025 a district court said the removals almost undoubtedly violated the notice rule and ordered no reinstatement.
rows.loop: Loop B1a: Independent oversight can limit policy favoritism

history-events.events_note: Every event here is graded documented: each rests on a statute, a court ruling, a constitutional text or another official record, cited in its source field. The grade covers the event itself; the size of any effect described in the mechanism comes from the scholarly or official source named beside it.
history-events.source_line: Oath & Action, Who Do They Answer To? Systems Atlas V7, history, 24 events. February 3, 1870 to June 29, 2026. United States. Snapshot of 2026-10-15. Each event rests on a statute, ruling, constitutional text or official record, cited in its own row; the size of any effect comes from the source named beside it.
notes: Event keys E01 to E24 are the studio's, in date order; V7 events carry no IDs.

numbers.caption: votes of 321,203: the margin by which Alaska's top-four primary survived a 2024 repeal measure, after a December 2024 recount. A second repeal measure, Ballot Measure 2, is on the ballot November 3, 2026.
numbers.qualification: The recount ended with 160,973 votes against repeal and 160,230 for it (Office of the Lieutenant Governor of Alaska, December 11, 2024).

numbers.caption: what pharmacies owned by the three largest pharmacy benefit managers (Caremark, Express Scripts and OptumRx) took in above their estimated cost to acquire 51 specialty generic drugs, 2017 to 2022
numbers.qualification: The figure counts revenue above acquisition cost; the Federal Trade Commission staff interim report (January 14, 2025) did not estimate profit. The FTC's separate insulin case is being resolved through proposed consent orders with Caremark and Express Scripts; as of October 15, 2026 neither order is final.

numbers.caption: a month: the cap on what people with Medicare Part D drug coverage pay out of pocket for each covered insulin since January 2023, under the Inflation Reduction Act
numbers.qualification: On March 1, 2023 Eli Lilly announced a $35 monthly cap on its insulins for people with commercial insurance or no insurance. The Federal Trade Commission's complaint of September 20, 2024 cites Humalog's list price as $21 in 1999 and more than $274 in 2017.

numbers.caption: inspectors general removed by email on January 24, 2025 without the 30 days' notice to Congress that the law requires
numbers.qualification: On September 24, 2025 a federal district court said the President almost undoubtedly violated the Inspector General Act and reinstated no one (Storch v. Hegseth). The latest public docket listing, dated July 22, 2026, shows no ruling on the merits.

numbers.caption: in financial benefits the Government Accountability Office reported for fiscal 2025
numbers.qualification: On September 24, 2025 a federal district court said the President almost undoubtedly violated the Inspector General Act and reinstated no one (Storch v. Hegseth). The latest docket entry listed, a July 20, 2026 minute order, shows no ruling on the merits.

numbers.caption: the child poverty rate under the Supplemental Poverty Measure in 2021, when the expanded child tax credit was in force, down from 9.7% in 2020; it was 13.4% in 2024 after the credit lapsed
numbers.qualification: These are the rates as first published. The Census Bureau revised its Supplemental Poverty Measure estimates for 2019 to 2024 in August 2026 after a correction to the poverty thresholds, and its report for 2025 came out September 15, 2026.
numbers.kind: evidence a rule changed an outcome

numbers.caption: of Republicans and of Democrats back a ban on stock trading by members of Congress
numbers.qualification: From a University of Maryland Program for Public Consultation survey of 2,625 registered voters (May 2023). The House passed a ban 232 to 198 on July 22, 2026. On September 30, 2026 the Senate fell short of the 60 votes needed to take it up, 53 to 47.

numbers.caption: of eligible voters cast the 2026 primary ballots that, by Unite America's count, effectively decided 88% of House seats (383 of 435)
numbers.qualification: Unite America, an advocacy group, built the count from Cook Political Report ratings (published September 16, 2026) and defines 'effectively decided' itself. Its 2024 figures (87% of seats, about 7%) used the voting-age population, so the two years are not directly comparable.

extras.homeownership_q2_2026_v7: Home equity is the main asset of middle-class households, and ownership rates differ: 74.5% of non-Hispanic white householders own their homes, 45.4% of Black householders and 48.1% of Hispanic householders (second quarter 2026). The same rise in house prices therefore moves each group's wealth differently.
